title: Demand-shaping token-bucket + queue prioritization sketch
content:
Context and intent:

This is an exploratory sketch for a demand-shaping + admission-control layer that lives between the global router and local region GPU pools. Goal: keep tail latency SLOs intact while maximizing throughput and utilization across multi-region, multi-capacity deployments (hosted + dedicated). This focuses on combining token-bucket rate shaping, queue-depth signals, and GPU utilization to make admission decisions and evict/redirect work proactively.

Notes / high-level requirements:
- Keep 99th pct latency stable for interactive routes (< 300ms target for small models, configurable per route).
- Prefer soft-admit with prioritized lanes (fast lane vs best-effort) rather than hard rejections for most customers.
- Support multi-region fallbacks: region-local -> nearby-region -> shared-dedicated -> graceful degrade (smaller model / quantized variant).
- Tight integration with control plane for capacity signals, heartbeat, and config push.
- Metering should map admission decisions to billing/chargeback (if we delay or route to cheaper capacity).

Core idea / components sketch:

1) Per-route token buckets (global + region-local view)
- Token buckets sit in the control plane router and at the regional admission proxy.
- Global token bucket enforces tenant-level allowed throughput (derived from account plan / Dedicated commit).
- Region-level token buckets are weighted by historical capacity and latency headroom. We compute a target replenishment rate R_region(route) from SLO, avg token cost (tokens per request depends on model seq len), and allocated GPUs.
- Token semantics: a token represents permission to dispatch the request to a GPU execution queue. Different request classes (sync vs streaming vs embedding) consume different token weights.

2) Queue-depth and per-GPU utilization signals
- Each regional pool publishes: queue_depth (per queue class), running_shards, GPU_util_1m, GPU_util_5m, evict_count, avg_batch_size.
- Local admission layer uses queue_depth + a moving-average GPU_util to adjust short-term token refill and to trigger soft-admit thresholds.
- Heuristic: if queue_depth > Q_high OR GPU_util_1m > U_high -> start shedding to lower-priority lanes or divert to fallback. If queue_depth < Q_low AND GPU_util_5m < U_low -> allow burst up to burst_tokens.

3) Priority lanes + soft-admit policy
- Lanes: premium (reserved for SLAs/dedicated), standard (default), best-effort (background transforms, lower QoS).
- Admission decision outputs: admit_local, queue_for_burst (short local buffer with timeout), redirect_to_nearby, fallback_model, reject (only as last resort).
- Soft-admit: we prefer queue_for_burst for a small, bounded time window (e.g., 200ms) rather than immediate redirect. This preserves locality and cache/KV benefits. If the bounded buffer overflows, escalate to redirect.

4) Multi-region routing coordination
- Control plane maintains per-region capacity snapshot with TTL (e.g., 5s). Regions push: available_slots_estimate, avg_latency, recent_evictions.
- Router scoring uses: latency_penalty, cost_penalty, capacity_headroom. Score = base + a*(est_latency/target) + b*(1 - headroom) + c*(cost_multiplier). Tunables a,b,c per tenant.
- When region is in 'stress' mode (rapid ramp in queue depth or GPU_util > 95%), prefer routing new sessions to other regions if score delta > threshold.

5) Token-bucket hierarchy and borrowing
- Hierarchy: global tenant bucket -> region bucket -> lane bucket. Tokens can be borrowed from region to serve short bursts if global budget permits. Conversely, region buckets can loan tokens to other regions via control-plane explicit transfer when utilization diverges persistently and network latency is low.
- Safety: borrowing must be reversible and instrumented; avoid oscillation by enforcing cooldown windows (e.g., 60s) and transferred token caps.

6) Fallback model selection and graceful degradation
- Fallbacks: smaller context windows, quantized model, or an alternative model family (faster but lower quality).
- Admission policy should encode quality constraints: only route to fallback if predicted quality drop < configured threshold for the route. Store per-route small eval sets to estimate impact.

7) Observability / metrics to expose
- Per-route: admitted_count, redirected_count, rejected_count, avg_queue_delay, avg_execution_latency, tokens_consumed, lane_breakdown.
- Per-region: queue_depth_histogram, gpu_util_pctiles, avg_batch_size, slow_start_events, borrow_in/out.
- Alerts: region_gpu_util > 98% sustained 30s, queue_depth > Q_critical for 15s, borrow_rate > X.

8) Control plane integration points
- Control plane provides: route configs (SLOs, lane priorities, token weights), region capacity snapshots, rollout of updated token refill rates, and centralized logging of admission events for audits.
- Push model: regions publish heartbeats (freq 2s) with capacity signals. Control plane pushes config changes with versioned policies, and admission proxies read local policy cache with graceful fallback to previous version on config fetch failure.

Implementation concerns / edge cases:
- Clock skew between control plane & region proxies: use logical counters and allow 1s slack on token expiry.
- Network partitions: if control plane unreachable, region should degrade to safe local policy (reserve 30% capacity for emergency requests and limit cross-region routing until restored).
- Inconsistent metrics: smoothing windows to avoid flip-flopping; limit policy changes to once per window (e.g., 5s).
- Fairness across tenants during high contention: implement weighted proportional fairness in token refill at the region level (weights from tenant commit).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Exact mapping from tokens -> compute slots for different model shapes (LLAMA2-70B vs LLaMA-7B). Need representative experiments (RED-4872).
- Borrowing thresholds and cooldown tuning: simulate with synthetic load traces.
- How to account for KV/prefix-cache locality when redirecting (latency hit vs cost savings). Could measure hit-rate degradation empirically.
- Billing mapping: when we redirect to cheaper dedicated pool or best-effort, how to propagate charges / attribution? Finance input needed.
- Security: cross-tenant isolation when borrowing capacity between tenants in the same pool - ensure no data leakage; likely require cryptographic isolation only at model layer.

Quick next steps (short-term):
- Write a simulation harness to model: token buckets + queue depth triggers + borrowing across 3-region topology (US-W, US-E, EU). Use past traffic traces to seed. (Owner: Elena)
- Instrument a canary regional proxy to emit the additional signals (queue_depth, avg_batch_size) to metrics pipeline. (Owner: Marcus)
- Prototype local admission logic in the router: lane selection + small burst buffer + redirect decision. Keep feature-flagged for 2 weeks. (Owner: Jordan)

References / related artifacts:
- RED-4872: modeling token-per-request for mixed workloads
- PR: serving-runtime#2145 - local queue metrics export
- Confluence: PlatformAdmissionDesign (sketch and prior notes)

Quick sketch (ASCII):

[Global Router] --(token check)-> [Region Proxy] --(queue)-> [GPU Pool]
                 \                       \-> redirect -> [Nearby Region Proxy]
                  \-> fallback -> [Quantized Fast Model Pool]

Endnotes: this is exploratory. Want to keep architecture minimal first (token buckets + queue-based shedding) and add borrowing once we have stable heuristics. Feedback welcome from SRE and runtime teams on failure modes and telemetry gaps.

Unresolved: name for the short-term local buffer — "burst queue" vs "soft-hold"? I prefer burst queue.
